md: Compare a multi-model router against the non-decreasing convex hull of the models it routes between, not against the strongest model. Beating GPT-4's price at GPT-4's quality is easy if a random mix of cheaper models already does it.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Matching descriptors and Lowe's ratio test
md: The ratio test needs at least two neighbors, so use `knnMatch(..., k=2)`. A matcher created with `crossCheck=True` is meant for `match()`, which returns one best match per descriptor.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The Michael-Scott queue: a dummy node and helping
md: Helping is the general trick for multi-step lock-free updates: leave the structure in a state that any thread can recognise as half-finished and complete on the owner's behalf. Then no thread ever needs to wait for a specific other thread.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: From templates to counts, time series and alerts
md: T3's baseline is all zeros, so its MAD is 0 and the modified z-score divides by zero. Never let a never-fired template be scored this way: handle it with a separate **first-seen** rule that alerts the first time a template id appears, or when a template's lifetime count crosses a small bound. A miner that reports a new template id gives you that signal for free.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: The detection lifecycle: hypothesis to retirement
md: An alert without a written response is a notification nobody owns. If you cannot say what the analyst should do in the first ten minutes, the detection is not finished.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Why models break past their trained length
md: Each RoPE pair has a wavelength $\lambda_d = 2\pi b^{2d/|D|}$. Pairs with $\lambda_d \ll L$ are safe at any length; pairs with $\lambda_d > L$ are the ones that break when you go past the trained window.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Attention memory and Ring Attention
md: Online softmax makes attention over KV blocks order-independent. Ring Attention exploits that: queries stay put, KV blocks travel around the ring, and each host needs memory proportional to its block, not to the full sequence.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Universal Transformers: recurrence over depth with a halting rule
md: Dynamic halting is not free accuracy. It helped on bAbI and LAMBADA but slightly hurt translation, adds a ponder-cost hyperparameter, and makes different positions in a batch finish at different times.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: When looping helps, when it hurts, and the design space
md: Looping buys **depth** (multi-step reasoning, using context), not **capacity** (memorized facts). Judge a looped model on reasoning tasks at matched FLOPs, not only on perplexity at matched parameters.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: QLoRA: fine-tuning on top of a 4-bit base model
md: QLoRA separates a storage type (NF4, 4 bits) from a compute type (BF16). Only the adapters are trained, so quantization error in the frozen base can be compensated by the adapters, and memory drops by about 4x versus a 16-bit base.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Approximate unlearning: gradient ascent, collapse and NPO
md: "Loss on the forget set went up" (or its perplexity, $e$ to the average per-token loss, as in the prerequisite course) is not evidence of good unlearning. GA can drive that loss arbitrarily high by wrecking the model. Always read forget metrics next to utility metrics and next to the retrained reference.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Lab: unlearn TOFU authors with NPO, measure it, then quantize it
md: Our run is one seed of a 124M model on 20 authors, with a simplified utility and our own simulated quantizer. Use it to learn the workflow and the failure modes, not as evidence about which method is better at scale; for that, run the framework and report its full metrics.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Persistence on macOS: launchd, login items and BTM
md: Look beyond launchd: Microsoft's Shrootless research showed `~/.zshenv` runs for every zsh, including under `sudo`. Shell startup files, login items and browser extensions are all persistence. A new agent is cheap for the attacker; your job is to make it loud.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: What malware is, and the families analysts name
md: Do not trust the malware's own story. A ransom note, a file name or an icon is chosen by the author. Classify by what the code actually does: NotPetya's note said ransomware, its code said wiper.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Dynamic analysis: sandboxes, monitors and the WannaCry kill switch
md: Never register or contact infrastructure from a live sample without authorisation and coordination. Hutchins' registration worked out, but researchers who touch attacker infrastructure can disrupt investigations or alert attackers. In your lab, the internet is fake by design.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Why vector size is a cost knob, and why chopping a vector fails
md: Matryoshka training puts the most useful information in the first coordinates, so a prefix of the vector is a good small embedding. Without it, keeping the first m numbers of a normal embedding throws away information almost at random.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Build it: pick a serving size and run a two-stage search on SciFact
md: Every query must be built exactly like the stored vectors: the same task prefix, the same layer norm, the same slice and the same bit rule. Each prefix size or precision you serve is its own index. In this run, skipping Nomic's layer norm changed nDCG@10 by at most 0.001, but other models and recipes may not be so forgiving.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Distributed optimizer and hiding communication behind compute
md: Overlap works because each collective has slack: gradients of late layers are ready early, and weights of the next layer are known before they are needed. What remains exposed is the last gradient bucket, the first parameter gather, and any collective on the critical path that cannot be chunked.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Acquiring RAM: WinPmem, DumpIt, LiME, AVML and virtual machines
md: Every acquisition changes the system it copies: the tool's process, its driver or module, and the memory they allocate all land in the image. LiME's README even warns that its optional digest and compression features disturb more of the target's memory. Record the tool, version, command and time so the footprint can be told apart from the attacker's.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Timelines from memory: what carries a time, and merging it
md: Memory gives you the start times of what is running now and a few remnants of what ran before. Disk gives you the long history. The overlap, a process in memory whose start matches a Prefetch run and a 4688 event, is where a timeline becomes solid.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Why freed memory does not go back: pages, arenas, purging
md: Setting `dirty_decay_ms` to 0 is not a free fix. The manual says it purges dirty pages immediately when they are created, so every page that empties pays for a purge, and every later reuse pays a page fault. It lowers RSS that is merely waiting; it does nothing for pages pinned by live objects.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Why freeing a removed node is the hard part
md: A garbage collector does not make ABA impossible in every case. Michael points out that if a program moves the same live node back and forth between two lists, ABA can still occur even with perfect GC. What a GC (and the schemes in this course) guarantees is narrower: a node's address is not reused while someone can still reach it.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Choosing a scheme: read cost versus bounded garbage
md: Grace periods (EBR, RCU) make reads cheap but let one stalled reader block all reclamation. Hazard pointers bound garbage at N x R but charge every visited node. Pick by read pattern and by how much you trust threads to keep moving.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Use-after-free and double free: dangling pointers
md: Chromium reports that about 70 percent of its high-severity security bugs are memory safety problems, and that half of those are use-after-free. Lifetimes are the hardest promise to keep by hand in a large C++ program.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Batch hard: mining the hardest pairs inside a P x K batch
md: Sample P identities x K images so every batch contains positives and look-alike negatives, then mine within the batch. Mining becomes a max and a min over a distance matrix you already have.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Measurement bias: layout, link order and JIT profiles
md: Misconception: "disabling ASLR and pinning the CPU makes my benchmark correct". They reduce run-to-run noise, which narrows intervals. A narrow interval around a biased setup is a confidently wrong answer.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Connecting an environment: rollout, generate and agent functions
md: Agent functions run in a child process of their own by default (`--custom-agent-function-mode subproc`), so one stuck episode cannot stall the others. The price: arguments and return values must be picklable, and module-level state lasts one call, so a module-level semaphore limits nothing. Use `rollout_semaphore` from `miles.rollout.agentic.rollout_limits`, or `inline` mode for debugging.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned policies leave a gap: LRU versus Belady's MIN
md: MIN is not a policy you can deploy, and it is not what learned caches try to predict exactly. It is a **yardstick**. Its value is telling you how big the gap is. On six production CDN traces with a 1 TB cache, the LRB authors measured a 25 to 40% gap in byte miss ratio (the fraction of requested bytes the cache could not serve) between MIN and the best online policies they tested.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Inside an APK and an IPA: what anyone can download and read
md: Legal note from the MASTG: in the US the DMCA (Digital Millennium Copyright Act, 17 U.S.C. 1201) makes circumventing some DRM illegal, with exemptions for certain security research. On a client engagement, ask the developer for unencrypted builds; it is faster and removes the question.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: The app is not the boundary: backend APIs seen through the app
md: A setting enforced only in the app's user interface is a display preference, not a privacy control. Test every privacy and permission setting by reading the raw API response.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Build an MLA layer and prove the two forms agree
md: Absorption is exact algebra, so a correct absorbed decoder matches the plain form to floating-point noise. Any larger gap is a bug, and the usual suspects are the norm, the RoPE split and the scale.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Thousands of adapters: S-LoRA's unified paging and loading
md: Unified Paging is not magic capacity. Adapter pages and KV pages come from the same pool, so many large adapters active at once shrink the space for KV cache and therefore the batch size. That is why clustering and rank choices still matter.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Why one phrasing of a question misses relevant documents
md: Retrieval quality depends on the exact words of the query. Multi-query retrieval treats the user's wording as one sample from many possible phrasings and retrieves with several samples instead of betting on one.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Bi-encoder, late interaction, cross-encoder: where the cost goes
md: Precompute versus interact. The more of the query-document comparison happens at query time, the more accurate and the more expensive the scorer. Bi-encoders and late interaction can serve as first stages over an index; cross-encoders only fit on short candidate lists.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Reusing the extra heads to decode faster
md: MTP gives two separate benefits: a training signal that can make the main model better, and heads that can draft tokens for exact, faster greedy decoding. You can use the first without the second by discarding the heads.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: SOAP: run Adam in the coordinates Shampoo discovers
md: SOAP = rotate into Shampoo's eigenbasis, run Adam there, rotate back. Refresh the rotation rarely; update Adam's statistics every step.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: What breaks in SP after a single training step
md: Random weights times activations grow like sqrt(n); updates times activations grow like n, because updates are correlated with the activations they act on. muP sets each layer's init and learning rate so that both effects stay order 1.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Transferring across depth: branch multipliers, Depth-muP, CompleteP
md: Width-only muP leaves the best LR drifting with depth. Scaling each residual branch by $L^{-\alpha}$, with AdamW block LRs scaled by $L^{\alpha-1}$, is the fix: Depth-muP's $\alpha = 1/2$ is one choice, but in CompleteP's pre-LN Transformer runs only $\alpha = 1$ kept the optimal HPs fixed across depth, and it keeps every layer learning features.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: Building a mutex on a futex: the three-state lock
md: A good futex mutex makes the uncontended path pure user space: one CAS to lock, one swap to unlock, zero system calls. The kernel is visited only when a thread really has to sleep, and unlock calls wake only if the word says someone might be sleeping.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Write skew: the bug that snapshot isolation lets through
md: Repeatable Read in PostgreSQL is not serializable. The docs warn that business rules enforced by transactions at this level are not likely to work correctly without explicit locks or the Serializable level.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Scoring whole sequences: transitions and Viterbi by hand
md: A CRF changes two things at once. At **training** time the loss is over whole sequences, so the model learns which label follows which. At **decoding** time Viterbi returns the best-scoring sequence rather than the best label at each position, so the output is a well-formed tag sequence by construction rather than by repair.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Attribution by governments: levels, confidence and evidence
md: Copy attribution wording exactly. "Almost certainly responsible" is not "proven"; "high confidence" in a group is not "high confidence" in the state behind it; a company's cluster name is not a government's finding. Upgrading a claim by paraphrase is the most common attribution error in briefs.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a state-threat brief, and practice
md: State cyber operations are strategy carried out through ordinary intrusion steps. Read the purpose, keep every attribution claim tied to its source and exact words, know which legal and diplomatic lines are being argued about, and turn it all into tested defences against the behaviours of the groups that matter to you.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Why MD5 misses copies, and the average hash that does not
md: A perceptual hash finds copies of *the same picture*, not *pictures of the same thing*. Two different photos of the same dog get unrelated hashes. For semantic similarity you need learned embeddings: vectors that a trained neural network outputs for each image, placed so that images with similar content land close together (lesson 5 covers one built for copies).

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Training backends (Automodel, Megatron) and generation backends
md: Training parallelism and generation parallelism are separate settings. For example vLLM's `tensor_parallel_size` is unrelated to Megatron's `tensor_model_parallel_size`. Refit must reshape weights from the trainer's layout into the engine's layout, which is part of why refit transports matter (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: RPKI and route origin validation
md: RPKI answers 'may this AS originate this prefix?'. It turns the most common hijack, a wrong origin or an unexpected more specific, into an Invalid route that validating networks drop. It does not validate paths or stop leaks with the correct origin.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Capturing at scale: taps, mirror ports, drops and retention
md: Monitoring captures other people's data. NIST SP 800-86 advises written policies on what may be monitored without approval, a formal request and approval process before recording a particular user's traffic, warning banners on systems, and rules for handling passwords or private messages that analysts see by accident. Capture only networks you own or are authorised to monitor.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Finding beacons with robust statistics: the RITA approach
md: Medians and quartiles let a beacon survive sleeps, reboots and network outages that wreck a mean. Score regularity robustly, then rank by rarity: a regular connection that only one machine in the company makes is the classic lead.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: IP addresses, subnets and CIDR
md: Prefix length decides everything: which addresses are "local" (same subnet, reached directly) and which need a router. If you can turn /27 into a network address, a broadcast address and a host count, you can read any firewall rule or scan scope.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Why some memory is farther away than other memory
md: Remote memory is not slow like disk. It is the same DRAM, reached through one more hop, typically tens of percent slower per miss. The bigger danger is usually *bandwidth*: when all hot data sits on one node, one memory controller serves every socket while the others idle.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Keeping threads near their data: pinning, balancing and diagnosis
md: Balancing is not free. The kernel docs say the unmapping and extra faults cost overhead that is *ideally* offset by better locality, with no universal guarantee, and that it should be disabled when the workload is already bound to NUMA nodes. Workloads that are already pinned and carefully placed are the natural candidates to turn it off.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Removing duplicates: greedy NMS and DETR's set prediction
md: Duplicates are handled either after the fact by NMS, a hand-tuned greedy filter on IoU, or during training by one-to-one Hungarian matching, which teaches the model itself to emit one box per object.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Committing to object storage: metadata, CAS and fencing
md: Leases and timeouts alone do not fence. A paused process cannot notice that its lease expired while it was paused, so its next write happens anyway. Safety comes from the **storage rejecting** the stale writer: a conditional PUT on a slot the new writer already claimed.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Cardinality: labels multiply, and a histogram multiplies again
md: Never put an unbounded set in a label. The naming guide names the usual offenders: do not use labels to store dimensions with high cardinality, such as user IDs, email addresses, or other unbounded sets of values. Raw URLs with query strings, trace ids, error message strings and timestamps belong on the same list.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Reading a line: CRNN features and CTC decoding
md: Merging repeats happens **before** removing blanks. Doing it in the other order would turn b - o - o k into b o o k and then merge the o's into 'bok'.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: SELinux: labels, types and the policy that decides
md: Two habits defeat SELinux: switching it to permissive "to make the app work", and feeding every denial to `audit2allow`, a tool that writes allow rules from log lines. The SELinux Notebook warns that new rules "may start opening holes". First ask whether the label is wrong (restorecon) or a boolean exists for the need.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: What OSINT is, and what it is for
md: OSINT is not "anything on the internet is fair game". Collecting and combining public facts about a private person to expose, harass or locate them is **doxxing** (publishing documents and personal details about someone) and can be a crime and is always a harm. This course does not teach it.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Mapping your own organisation's public footprint
md: Point OSINT at yourself first. Registration data, DNS, certificate logs, search engines, code hosts and job adverts together describe what an attacker sees; an inventory diffed on a schedule turns that into findings.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Archiving: capturing evidence that will still be trusted later
md: Capture URL, source, full-page image and media; record who, when (UTC, synced clock) and why; hash every file at collection; keep a read-only copy.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: CMake in three phases: configure, generate, build
md: `cmake -S . -B build` configures and generates; `cmake --build build` runs the native tool. Settings live in `build/CMakeCache.txt` and persist until you change them, remove them, or use `--fresh`.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Why flaky tests ruin big suites: the probability
md: Retrying until green is not fixing. The same math that removes noise also removes signal from real intermittent bugs, and concurrency bugs are exactly the ones that fail intermittently. Google's post makes a related point about its own fail three times in a row policy: it reduces false positives but encourages developers to ignore flakiness and delays finding real breakages.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: GitHub mechanics: decisions, suggestions and merge rules
md: Do not resolve a reviewer's thread you disagreed with and did not change. Collapsing a thread hides it from the list of open conversations, so silently resolving an open disagreement reads as ignoring it. Reply, and resolve only when the thread is truly finished.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Codes of conduct: scope, reporting and the enforcement ladder
md: Default to public communication, with two exceptions: security vulnerabilities and serious conduct violations. Each has its own documented private channel; find it before you need it.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Folding review fixes into the right commit with --fixup
md: `git commit --fixup=X` then `git rebase -i --autosquash BASE` puts a fix into commit X without editing the todo list by hand. Every commit after X gets a new hash.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Copyleft: when you must share source, and with whom
md: Copyleft obligations trigger on conveying: giving someone a copy. AGPL is the exception that also counts remote network use of a modified version.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Noise and bias: making before and after comparable
md: A small, very stable difference can still be a layout accident: your patch moved code, and alignment changed. If a 1 to 2% win appears in code you did not expect to matter, rebuild with a different layout (the paper calls this setup randomization) or test on another machine before claiming it.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: git blame: who last changed a line, and seeing past noise
md: blame only describes lines that exist now. The manual is explicit: the report does "not tell you anything about lines which have been deleted or replaced". If you want to know when a check was removed, blame cannot answer; the next lesson's pickaxe can.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: git bisect: finding the commit that introduced the bug
md: A fast, exact repro turns history into a binary search: about $\log_2 N$ automated tests to find the commit that introduced the bug, and naming that commit in your report saves the maintainer hours.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: A title and description that explain why
md: Title: what the change does, short enough for one-line views. Body: the problem and its impact, the approach, where to look, what you left out, and links. The description outlives the review: Google notes it may be read by hundreds of people over the years.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Sharing blocks with reference counts and copy-on-write
md: A physical block may back many logical blocks. Reference counts say when it can be freed; copy-on-write makes writes into shared blocks safe, at the cost of copying one block.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Prefix caching across a fleet and behind an API
md: In a fleet the hit rate is decided before any engine sees the request: routing must send a prefix where its KV lives, balanced against load, and the router must learn where KV lives from guesses or from engine events. Cache scope (per user, organization or global) is a privacy decision, not just a performance one.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Verifying findings safely, without becoming the incident
md: Verify with the least risky evidence that answers the question. Write down the confidence and what you chose not to do. Stop immediately when you see signs that someone else got there first.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Broken stacks: frame pointers, DWARF, LBR and symbols
md: Missing callers, a detached tower over [unknown], or hex instead of names are not hot spots. They are profiler blind spots. Fix frame pointers or symbols before you trust the picture.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Why people are the most attacked surface
md: The one thing to remember: phishing attacks a decision, not a machine. Defences therefore come in three kinds: stop the message arriving, make the action harmless if taken (for example passkeys, logins that only work on the real site; lesson 12), and make the final step need a second check (for example calling the supplier on a known number).

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Lookalike domains and homoglyphs
md: Misconception: "hover over the link and check the domain" solves this. A homoglyph domain can look correct even when you hover, and on phones you often cannot hover. Machine checks (skeletons, domain age) and phishing-resistant logins (lesson 12) carry the load; human checks are a backup.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Byte order: reading and writing multi-byte fields on the wire
md: Wire formats fix two things: where each field sits and the byte order inside it. Pick the order in the format's specification, then convert at the edge with shifts, `from_be_bytes` or `ntohl`, and keep ordinary structs inside the program.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Real-time tracking, 3D lifting and joint angles for apps
md: Keypoints are noisy, especially when occluded. Before writing rules on them: check per-keypoint visibility or score, prefer 3D world landmarks or a side view for sagittal angles (bends in the side-view plane that splits the body into left and right) such as the knee, smooth over a few frames, and use two thresholds (hysteresis) rather than one.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Crypto inventory and agility: finding every RSA before 2030
md: Agility has a price you met in tls-pki: anything that negotiates can be **downgraded**. Keep the allowed list short, remove algorithms rather than leaving them enabled "just in case", and authenticate the negotiation (as TLS 1.3 does by signing the transcript). An unauthenticated algorithm field is an attacker's choice, not yours.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Estimating selectivity, and correlated filters
md: A planner's match count says nothing about correlation. Two filters with the same s can need about 30 candidates or 8,500. If a filter's meaning is tied to the embedding (a topic, a language, a source), expect it to be correlated with queries, positively for some and negatively for others.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Bandwidth-bound code: count the bytes, skip the reads
md: Do not sprinkle streaming stores everywhere. Intel recommends them for memset-style fills larger than about half the last-level cache when the data is not read soon after. On Skylake server it warns that overusing them on smaller blocks evicts lines you need and can hit a per-core limit on non-temporal write bandwidth.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: k-anonymity: generalise and suppress until you hide in a crowd
md: k-anonymity is a property of one table against one declared set of quasi-identifiers. It says nothing about columns you forgot, other releases, or what the sensitive values in a class reveal.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Differential privacy in real systems: units, trust and hazards
md: "We use differential privacy" is not a guarantee until you know three things: epsilon (and delta), the unit of privacy, and who sees the raw data. A large epsilon at event level with a trusted curator can protect very little.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Private set intersection: comparing lists without sharing them
md: Diffie-Hellman PSI works because blinded exponentiation commutes: H(x)^(ab) = H(x)^(ba). Each side blinds with a secret it never reveals, so only matching items line up. Hashing alone is not PSI, because hashes of small identifier spaces can be inverted.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Linux escalation 1: reading sudo rules like an auditor
md: Misconception: "NOPASSWD is the dangerous part." It does remove a hurdle for an intruder who has a shell but not the password (a web shell, a stolen SSH key). But a rule that leads to a shell is a root grant with or without a password prompt. Fix what the command can do first, then decide on the password.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: How a PRM is trained and how it scores a solution
md: A PRM is a per-step classifier read off in one forward pass. Training labels stop at the first error. To compare solutions you reduce step scores to one number; product and minimum perform similarly, but product quietly favours shorter solutions.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Generative PRMs: verifiers that reason before they judge
md: Generative PRMs phrase verification as text generation: write a step-by-step critique, then read the verdicts and a Yes probability off it. They need far fewer labels and lead on error location, at the price of many more tokens per verification and overconfident scores.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Counting switches and designing around them
md: Misconception: "more threads means more parallelism." Parallelism is capped by the number of cores. Past that, extra CPU-bound threads only take turns: they add involuntary switches, push answers later, and make threads evict each other's cache. Extra threads help only when they spend time blocked, as in the I/O scene.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: DSPy: signatures, modules and optimizers
md: Every bootstrap and search optimizer trusts the metric. The DSPy docs warn that a non-deterministic metric (for example an LLM judge) makes the chosen demos "a function of metric noise as much as program quality". Make the metric deterministic where you can, validate any LLM judge against humans first, and keep a held-out set.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Why security teams script, and your first Python program
md: A script is the steps you would do by hand, written down once so they run the same way on every line. Its biggest risk is not crashing; it is quietly counting the wrong thing.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Hashing files and checking them against known-bad lists
md: Hash files in binary chunks, normalize every indicator to lowercase before comparing, and remember that a match means "known bad" while a miss means only "not this exact file".

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym filters in Elasticsearch and OpenSearch
md: Create the synonym set before the index that references it. Elastic's guide warns that an index pointing at a missing set becomes inoperable and must be deleted and re-created, or closed and re-opened.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Conversational rewriting: turning a follow-up into a standalone query
md: Misconception: the rewriter should make the query richer. Its job is to make it *standalone and faithful*. A rewriter that adds guessed facts (say, "when the leader fails during a network partition") can steer retrieval toward documents the user never asked about. Instruct it not to answer, and to return the message unchanged when it is already standalone.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Computing the estimate with popcount, and re-ranking by the bound
md: Per vector, the query-time work is a few AND plus popcount passes over the D-bit code and a handful of multiply-adds with precomputed factors. The error bound then tells you which candidates are worth an exact distance.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Race conditions from zero: concurrency, the race window and TOCTOU
md: A lock inside one process (threading.Lock here) protects only threads in that process. A web app with several worker processes or servers needs the lock where the state lives, usually in the database (lesson 9).

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Why "too fast to exploit" fails: jitter and the single-packet attack
md: The single-packet attack made network distance irrelevant: a tester far away can now hit a 1 ms window about as reliably as one on the same network. Treat every check-then-act as reachable, and fix it with atomicity, not with speed.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft log replication: AppendEntries, nextIndex and commit
md: Stored on a majority is not the same as committed. An entry from an *earlier* term can sit on a majority and still be erased by a later leader. Commitment is only decided by counting replicas of an entry from the leader's *current* term, which then commits everything before it.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: What a ranker sees: one feature vector per query-document pair
md: A ranking model only knows what its feature vector tells it. If a signal that decides relevance (freshness for news, location for local search) is not encoded as a number for each query-document pair, no amount of model tuning can recover it.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: ERR: a user who stops once satisfied
md: **$g_{\max}$ is a convention, and tools hard-code it.** TREC's `gdeval.pl` (the official Web track script, which ir_measures used for `ERR@5` in our test) sets `MAX_JUDGMENT = 4`. With our 0 to 3 grades, gdeval gives Run A an ERR@5 of 0.240, not 0.452, and Run B 0.438, not 0.875. Rankings of runs may survive, but the numbers cannot be compared with an ERR computed under $g_{\max} = 3$.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Case: Change Healthcare and ALPHV, February 2024
md: One remote access portal without MFA, at one subsidiary, gave a criminal nine quiet days. Inventory every remote access path (VPNs, Citrix, RDP gateways, vendor portals, acquired companies' systems) and enforce MFA on all of them, then test that it is enforced.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Memory registration: pinning, translation and keys
md: An (address, rkey) pair is a capability: whoever holds it, on a QP in the same protection domain, can read or write that memory with no further check by your CPU. Grant the narrowest access flags you need, and revoke by deregistering (`ibv_dereg_mr`) or with memory windows, which the manual describes as a cheaper way to grant and revoke remote access dynamically.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Client-side prediction and server reconciliation
md: Each server state is a statement about the past: "here is the world after your input #n". Reset to it, then replay inputs after #n. Sequence numbers are what make that subtraction possible.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Two-stage systems: candidate generation, two towers, ranking
md: Retrieval must be cheap per item (dot products over precomputed vectors); ranking can be expensive per item. In-batch negatives are sampled by popularity, so correct each logit by log p_j.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: A query plan is a tree of operators that pull rows
md: Cost units are not milliseconds. They are relative estimates the planner uses to compare plans. To see real time, use EXPLAIN ANALYZE, which actually runs the query.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Leader replication: when is a commit really safe?
md: A commit is only as safe as the set of machines that had it when the client was told "ok". Every replication knob is a choice of *how many* and *which* machines that set must include, paid for in commit latency.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: What RLHF reward hacking looks like: length, sycophancy, persuasion
md: Misconception: longer answers after RLHF just mean a more helpful model. Sometimes length carries real information. But when the reward gain mostly vanishes once you compare answers of equal length, the policy has optimized a correlate of quality, not quality. Report output length next to every reward and win rate.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Governance, risk and compliance: three jobs and who decides
md: A common misconception: "security owns security risk". In every framework in this course, the **business owner** of a system owns its risk and the decision to accept it. The security team advises, measures and challenges. When security silently accepts risk on the business's behalf, nobody with budget or authority knows the risk exists.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Treating risk: accept, mitigate, transfer, avoid
md: Every risk ends in one of four decisions, recorded with an owner and a date. Compare options in money: expected yearly loss plus treatment cost for the average, and tail percentiles for survival. Mitigation usually wins on average; insurance wins on the tail; avoidance can win on both.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: PCI DSS v4: the cardholder data environment and scoping
md: PCI DSS is a contractual standard with 12 requirements. Scope is the CDE plus anything connected to it or able to affect it, so reduce scope first: segment, and better, never touch card numbers (tokenise with a payment provider). What remains on your side, especially the payment page's scripts, must be inventoried and watched.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Policies people follow and awareness that works
md: Policies: short, owned, true, enforced by guardrails, with an exception path and a review date. Awareness: required by every framework, but measure it honestly; put the weight on controls that make human mistakes survivable, and on making reporting easy.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: The long tail: why one response can idle a whole cluster
md: Partial rollouts are not free. A trajectory stitched from segments generated by several policy versions is off-policy data. Kimi notes some segments can be excluded from the loss; AReaL's interruptible rollouts face the same issue and handle it with a modified PPO objective.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Multi-turn agentic rollouts: tools, servers and token-in, token-out
md: Agentic rollouts move the bottleneck from decode length to tool latency. Run each trajectory as its own coroutine against continuous-batching servers, route a conversation's turns to the same server, scale tools as separate services, and pass exact token ids and logprobs to the trainer.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: MTTR: detect, triage, mitigate, resolve
md: Mitigating destroys evidence. Reverting the config drains the queue, restarts pods and rotates the logs that held the smoking gun. Before you revert, spend the 30 seconds: snapshot the pool metrics, grab one stack dump, copy the rendered config, note the exact timestamps. The chapter's phrase is that rapid triage does not preclude preserving evidence of what is going wrong.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Weighted RRF and multi-query fusion (RAG-Fusion)
md: Multi-query fusion has costs. In the Infineon study RAG-Fusion averaged 34.62 s versus 19.52 s for plain RAG (1.77 times slower in that deployment), mostly from the larger answer call, and some answers strayed off topic when the generated queries were not relevant enough. If the rewrites are near-duplicates, fusion just re-counts the same list.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: From -ENOMEM and ERR_PTR to Result
md: `to_result` is not a general converter. For a C function that returns a byte count or an index on success, use the raw value: check `< 0` yourself or write a small wrapper that returns `Result<usize>`. Otherwise the success value silently disappears.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The baseline you replace: EEVDF picks and the knobs it offers
md: Misconception: a shorter slice buys a task more CPU. Under EEVDF it buys an earlier deadline and more, shorter turns; the total still follows the weights.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Build, load and run your own scheduler end to end
md: Misconception: the loader is just a launcher and can exit once the scheduler is attached. The link belongs to the process: when it exits, the link is destroyed and the kernel unregisters the scheduler. The loader is also the only place the exit reason gets printed.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Measuring and debugging a scheduler
md: Misconception: a lower average latency means a better scheduler. A policy can cut the median and still multiply the p99, and for interactive work the tail is what users feel.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Case: Storm-0558 and a signing key that should have died in 2021
md: A signing key's real lifetime is not what the plan says but what the system enforces. Enforce expiry in code, alert on key age, and treat "we paused rotation" as a security incident with an owner and a deadline.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: JavaScript: prototype pollution and code built from strings
md: Pollution is process-wide and lasts until restart. One request can change the behaviour of every later request to that Node.js process, including other users' requests, which makes it confusing to debug and dangerous to leave running.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Heartbleed as a diff: reviewing every field of a message
md: Field checklist for any parser diff: list every value taken from outside, and for each one point to the line that validates it against a fact the code controls (the real buffer length, a maximum). An empty cell is a finding. For pointer loops, end checks use < or >=, never == or !=.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Secure channels at every layer: what each protocol protects
md: Ask two questions of any secure protocol: between which two points does the protection start and stop, and what happens to the data outside them? A VPN stops at the gateway; SSH stops at the server process; S/MIME never stops while the message stays encrypted.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Time is a security input: NTP, delay attacks and NTS
md: NTS stops forged and altered time replies; it cannot stop delay attacks, because a delayed packet is still authentic. RFC 8915 bounds the damage at MAXDIST/2 and suggests several time sources or several network paths. Combine NTS with multiple servers and alert on large clock steps.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: The perimeter model, Operation Aurora and the road to BeyondCorp
md: Zero trust does not mean "no VPN" or "no firewall". BeyondCorp removed the trust that came with being on the network. Encrypted tunnels and network filters still exist in zero trust designs; they just stop being the reason anyone gets access.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Measuring the journey: CISA's maturity model and a migration plan
md: A maturity score measures capabilities, not outcomes. An agency can be Advanced in every pillar and still be breached through an unpatched edge appliance. Track both: the stage per pillar, and evidence such as how many apps still need a VPN and how many accounts still use phishable MFA.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Worked scenario: prompt injection through attacker-written log fields
md: Anything an attacker can write into a log can end up in your model's context. Give the model no authority the attacker should not have, let deterministic rules make decisions, and treat instruction-like text in a field as an indicator.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Attack surface, and the Morris worm's four doors
md: Attack surface is everything an attacker can touch: services, features, trust relationships and people. The Morris worm used all four kinds at once. The cheapest defence is removing doors you do not need (a debug command in production, an unused service); the next is making each remaining door check its input.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The attack lifecycle: kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK
md: Real attacks do not walk the phases neatly in order. Attackers loop (discover, move, discover again), skip steps (a stolen password needs no weaponization), and run phases in parallel. Use the models as a vocabulary and a checklist, not a script.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Building a programme from zero: the first 90 days
md: Do not promise a compliance date (a SOC 2 report, an ISO certificate) before you know the current state. Recall that SOC 2 Type II needs a period of operating evidence: a date picked in week one becomes a commitment you may have to break publicly.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Metrics that drive decisions, and how targets corrupt them
md: Choose a few metrics that map to decisions: implementation for rollout, effectiveness and efficiency for whether controls work, impact for executives. Pair each target with a metric that would reveal gaming, measure what is still open, and make the things that matter part of how leaders are judged.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Rebuilding after failure: Equifax, Maersk and Microsoft
md: Beware survivorship and self-reporting. You read about rebuilds that companies chose to describe; failed rebuilds rarely get Senate testimony. Figures such as "35,000 engineers" or "USD 1.25 billion" are the companies' own, with their own definitions. Use them as examples of levers, not as benchmarks.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Getting a fix shipped when you cannot order it
md: Escalation is not a weapon. If owners learn that talking to security means being reported upward, they stop talking to security, and you lose the early warnings that matter most. Agree the path in advance, use it predictably, and make the first step always a direct conversation.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Build a STaR loop: sample, filter, fine-tune, repeat
md: Measure the filter, not just the score. Two cheap audits caught what accuracy alone hid: check an intermediate quantity on a sample of kept data, and track held-out accuracy every iteration, since training accuracy rises regardless.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Choosing the threshold: hit rate against false hits
md: Do not copy a threshold from a tutorial or a library default. Collect a few hundred real pairs from your traffic, label whether the cached answer would be correct, and pick the threshold from that data and your cost of a wrong answer (lesson 5 does this on a public dataset). Re-check whenever you change the embedding model, since similarity scales differ between models.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Why cloud metadata is the prize: Capital One 2019
md: "It is in a private subnet" does not protect a role's credentials. Temporary credentials from IMDS work from anywhere on the internet unless a policy restricts where they can be used. The attacker used them from their own machine.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: LM programs: why the runtime should see the whole program
md: Misconception: "SGLang is a prompt DSL, so I must rewrite my app to use it." A DSL, or domain-specific language, is a small language built for one kind of job, here writing LM programs. Most of SGLang's speedups live in the runtime and apply to plain HTTP requests. The DSL is an optional layer on top.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Prefill-decode disaggregation and speculative decoding in SGLang
md: PD disaggregation and speculation attack different stalls. PD keeps prefill out of decode steps at the price of GPUs and a KV transfer; speculation turns idle compute during memory-bound decode into extra tokens per step, and pays off most at low concurrency.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Real engines: turn costs, live traffic and time-dependent travel
md: Production routing = a graph from OSM (directed, with turn costs) + a preprocessing technique. CH gives the fastest queries on a fixed metric; partition-based MLD or CRP accepts new weights in seconds without redoing the expensive phase.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Why speedups fall short: latency chains and the memory wall
md: Two ceilings limit SIMD: latency chains (fix with several independent accumulators) and memory bandwidth (fix by doing more work per byte or keeping data in cache). Lane count only matters once both are out of the way.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Bump allocation: a bounds check and a pointer add
md: Bump allocation costs a few instructions and has no per-object free. It is ideal when a group of objects share one lifetime (a request, a frame, a compiler pass) and wrong when objects die at unrelated times, because one long-lived object keeps the whole arena alive.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Low-precision rollout: FP8 weights, FP8 KV cache and INT4
md: INT4 checkpoints use a `compressed-tensors` config whose `ignore` list also steers online quantization. The debug guide's example: if the MoE router `mlp.gate.weight` is not ignored, slime INT4-quantizes it, SGLang does not expect quantized names for the router and silently skips them, and the router weights end up all zeros. `--check-weight-update-equal` (lesson 3) catches this.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Train-rollout mismatch in slime: TIS, IcePop, R3 and score centering
md: slime treats SGLang as a behavior policy q. TIS caps the correction, IcePop drops out-of-band tokens, R3 removes MoE routing flips at the source, and score centering repairs the baseline. All need rollout log probs on every sample, and all are judged by the same few metrics.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Inside the EVM: storage, calls, msg.sender and delegatecall
md: CALL: their code, their storage. DELEGATECALL: their code, **your** storage and your money. Treat every delegatecall target as if it were your own code, because in effect it is.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: What a SOC is, and what an analyst does all day
md: An alert is a question, not an answer. The analyst's job is to answer it with evidence, record the answer so someone else can check it, and feed what was learned back into the rules.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Phishing reports and unusual data egress
md: Volume alone is a weak signal; volume against the host's own baseline, plus the sending process and the destination's owner, is a strong one. Exfiltration to a popular cloud storage service will look normal by destination, so the process and the account doing the upload matter most.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Warnings people heed: browser warnings and opinionated design
md: Warnings work when they are rare, specific and opinionated, and fail when they are frequent and neutral. Where the safe answer is always the same, block instead of warning.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Dropped USB drives, implants and unattended screens
md: Misconception: "it's only dangerous if someone opens a file on the drive". Devices that present themselves as a keyboard can type commands as soon as they are connected, and a network implant needs no user action at all. Controls must act at connection time.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Training at scale: dead latents and feature splitting
md: Dead latents grow with width; fix them with resampling, encoder-equals-decoder-transpose init and an AuxK loss. Feature splitting means the dictionary you get depends on width, so a feature is always 'a feature at this resolution'.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: train a TopK SAE on GPT-2, then use a released one
md: A working SAE pipeline is: cache a site with BOS dropped, shuffle, normalise by one scalar, train with transposed init and unit decoder columns (plus AuxK at scale), then judge it by L0, FVU and delta LM loss from splicing. A released SAE plus Neuronpedia gets you to reading and steering in a few lines.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in map coordinates
md: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in 2D or 3D coordinates. Simple kriging is the zero-mean GP on residuals; ordinary kriging adds an unknown constant mean; universal kriging adds trend basis functions; the nugget is observation noise.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Drafting without a second model: Medusa heads and token trees
md: Not every tree method is lossless. Medusa's optional **typical acceptance** keeps a candidate if the target's probability exceeds $\min(\epsilon, \delta e^{-H(p)})$, a threshold that depends on the entropy $H$. It raises speed at higher temperatures but no longer samples from the target's distribution. Medusa-2 also changes the backbone weights, so outputs differ from the original model.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Word error rate: alignments, normalization and fair comparisons
md: Only compare WER numbers computed with the same normalizer on the same references. Switching normalizers, or counting *you're* versus *you are* as an error, can move WER more than a model upgrade. For languages written without spaces, character error rate (CER) is used instead.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The heap: free lists, chunk headers and where malloc gets memory
md: Stack: LIFO, bounded, freed by returning, one instruction. Heap: any order, any size, any lifetime, paid for with headers, rounding, free-list searches and fragmentation.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Page faults: lazy allocation, copy-on-write and overcommit
md: Most page faults are normal: they are how Linux allocates memory on first touch and copies pages only on write. Count them with getrusage or `perf stat -e page-faults,major-faults`; worry about major faults and fault storms, not their existence.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: When steering fails: unreliable inputs and the prompting baseline
md: Steering is a research and monitoring tool before it is a product control. Use it when you need to know *which* internal direction drives a behavior, to detect a concept, or to add to a prompt (CAA's vectors still moved behavior on top of system prompts). Always report per-input effects, a random vector of equal norm and a prompting baseline; without them a mean effect proves little.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Downsampling, retention and exactly-once vs at-least-once
md: End-to-end exactly-once needs three parts: a replayable source (Kafka offsets), consistent state (checkpoints), and an output that is transactional or idempotent (upsert by a deterministic key such as sensor and window). Duplicates created upstream, such as MQTT QoS 1 retries, must be removed by id.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Multi-head attention by hand: two heads, two patterns
md: Multi-head attention = several narrow attention functions in parallel, each free to learn a different pattern, at roughly the cost of one wide head.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Why raw TF-IDF ranks a keyword-stuffed page first
md: BM25 is still a sum over query terms of (IDF) x (a term-frequency factor). What changes is the term-frequency factor: it is bounded and length-aware instead of a raw count.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Which BM25? Variants, library differences and what they change
md: When you compare against a published BM25 number, match the variant, k1 and b, the analyzer (tokenizer, stop words, stemmer) and the field setup. The variant is usually the least important of these; the analyzer and parameters are usually the most.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule
md: Never compare losses across tokenizers. 1.47 nats per *character* and 2.85 nats per *BPE token* measure different things: a BPE token covers several characters, so it is much harder to predict. The released GPT-2 scores 3.12 on OWT partly because it was trained on WebText, not OpenWebText; nanoGPT notes that fine-tuning it on OWT brings it to about 2.85.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Integrals: accumulated change and area under a curve
md: A density value is not a probability, so it can be larger than 1. A density squeezed onto a narrow range must be tall to keep its total area at 1: spread evenly over an interval of width 0.5, its height is 2. Only areas under a density are probabilities.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Second derivatives, the Hessian and the shape of a minimum
md: The Hessian holds the curvature in every direction. Its eigenvalues classify a critical point (all positive: minimum; mixed signs: saddle), the largest one sets the stable learning rate $2/\lambda_{\max}$, and their ratio sets how slowly gradient descent converges.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Writing scripts: arguments, tests, if, loops and functions
md: Inside `[ ]`, quote every variable: `[ "$x" = foo ]`. An empty or spaced value otherwise changes how many arguments `[` receives, and the test fails with an error instead of returning false. Inside `[[ ]]` a variable needs no quotes, except on the right of `==` or `=~`: there quotes make the pattern literal, so `[[ $f == "*.log" ]]` matches only a file named `*.log`.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly
md: Status 0 means success; 128 + N means killed by signal N. Start scripts with `set -euo pipefail`, quote every expansion, send errors to fd 2, and exit non-zero on failure so the next tool in the chain can tell.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: What the geometry means: cosine, analogies and PMI
md: Vector arithmetic analogies are a nice demo, not a law. The answer depends on excluding inputs, and Nissim et al. show that other implementation choices (casing, frequency cutoffs, the exact formula) change results too. The same arithmetic surfaces social biases: Bolukbasi et al. (2016) found that the GoogleNews word2vec vectors complete *man : computer programmer :: woman : x* with *homemaker*.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Math-bound or memory-bound: arithmetic intensity and the roofline
md: Intensity counts HBM traffic, not every load. Good kernels tile data into shared memory and registers so each HBM byte is reused many times; a naive kernel that re-reads HBM has a much lower effective intensity than the formula suggests.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Batching: sharing each weight read across many users
md: Bigger batches are not free for users: once the step leaves the flat region (math roof, or growing KV reads), every sequence's inter-token latency rises. A throughput number without a latency number hides this.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Bits, bytes and hex: how numbers are stored
md: Misconception: "signed overflow wraps in C too." The hardware adder wraps, but in C, overflowing a signed integer is [undefined behavior](https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/language/operator_arithmetic), and compilers optimize on the assumption that it never happens. Only unsigned arithmetic is guaranteed to wrap modulo $2^n$.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why memory is slow and how caches hide it
md: Performance is often decided by memory access patterns, not instruction counts. Touch memory sequentially, reuse data while it is still in cache, and keep hot data small.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: From web crawl to training tokens: the pretraining data pipeline
md: Raw crawl becomes training data through extraction, filtering, near-duplicate removal, PII and contamination handling, then packing. Each step was chosen by training small models on the result, and a run then moves through stages: main pretraining, context extension, annealing.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: RL with PPO: maximize reward, stay close to the SFT model
md: RLHF does not maximize reward. It maximizes reward minus beta times the KL from the SFT model, and beta sets how far the model may move to chase the reward model.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Phrase and proximity queries with a positional index
md: A positional index stores, for each term and document, the list of positions. A phrase or proximity query merges on docID first and then compares positions inside each shared document, so it costs work per occurrence, not just per document.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Inverted indexes in real engines: compression, updates, Lucene
md: TF-IDF still has two flaws that cosine only partly fixes: tf keeps growing with every repetition (keyword stuffing pays), and length normalization is crude. BM25, the next course, keeps the same inverted index and replaces the weighting with a saturating tf and a tunable length normalization.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Addresses and pointers: what int *p actually stores
md: A pointer is a variable whose value is an address. `&` takes an address, `*` follows one, and the pointer's type decides how many bytes are read or written at that address.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Structs and linked data: ->, typedef and a linked list
md: A struct is a named group of members; `.` selects a member and `->` selects one through a pointer. A linked list is nodes on the heap connected by pointers, and changing a list means rewriting the right link, which is why functions that change it take `node **`.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Debugging C: gdb and Valgrind on a real crash
md: Build with `-g -O0` when debugging. Read a backtrace from frame #0 down to your own code, then use breakpoints, next, step, finish and print to see why the state went wrong. Use watchpoints for 'who changed this', and Valgrind when you cannot rebuild.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Ownership in methods and loops: self, &self, &mut self and for
md: A method signature is an ownership contract: `&self` reads, `&mut self` modifies, `self` consumes. A `for` loop over `v` consumes it; over `&v` or `&mut v` it borrows.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Closures and threads: moving ownership to another thread
md: Adding `move` fixes E0373 by handing the value over, not by sharing it: the spawning function loses access. If both sides need the data, clone it before the spawn, or share it with `Arc`.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Matrix multiplication: composing maps and checking shapes
md: $(m \times n)(n \times p) = (m \times p)$. Each entry is a row-column dot product, the product means apply the right matrix first, and order matters.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Where it shows up: linear layers, batches and attention scores
md: Shape errors are the most common bug in ML code. Before running a line like `X @ W.T + b`, write the shapes next to it, `(B,n) @ (n,m) + (m,)`, and check that inner sizes match and the bias length equals the output size.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Classification end to end: logistic regression, boundaries and softmax
md: Do not apply softmax before passing scores to `CrossEntropyLoss`. It would softmax them a second time, squashing the probabilities toward each other and weakening the gradients. Pass the raw logits.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Measuring a model: metrics, thresholds and cross-validation
md: Accuracy on imbalanced data is close to meaningless: always compare it with the "always the majority class" baseline. Report precision and recall (or a PR curve) for the rare class.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: What hidden units compute: hinges, cuts and new features
md: Misconception: universal approximation means one wide layer is all you need. It says suitable weights exist, not how many units that takes or that gradient descent will find them. The notes of CS231n, Stanford's course on convolutional neural networks for visual recognition, call it mathematically cute but a relatively weak statement in practice.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Training a real network: an MLP on handwritten digits
md: Nothing new happened here. The forward pass, softmax cross-entropy, BP1 to BP4 in batched form and the SGD step are the same ones you ran by hand on a 2-2-1 network; MNIST just has 79,510 parameters and 64 examples per batch.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency: race conditions and locks
md: Any read-modify-write (read a value, change it, write it back) of shared data (even `x++`) is several instructions, and a context switch can split them. Protect every critical section with a lock, and build locks on atomic hardware instructions, never on plain loads and stores.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Files and directories: the API and how vsfs finds your data
md: lseek() never moves the disk head. It only changes the offset stored in the open file table. A disk seek happens later, if the next read or write lands on a different track.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayes' rule: why a 90 percent accurate test is often wrong
md: Posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior. Strong evidence can be overwhelmed by a small prior, and the denominator just rescales so the posteriors sum to 1.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence
md: Check the log base before comparing numbers. Machine learning code and the Deep Learning book use the natural log (nats); information theory texts often use bits. Divide nats by $\ln 2 = 0.693$ to get bits.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Why loss falls on a straight line in log-log space
md: A scaling law turns each multiplicative step in scale into a fixed **ratio** of loss. Fit the exponent on cheap runs, then extrapolate. Small exponents (around 0.05 to 0.1 here) mean big scale-ups buy modest gains.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Inference cost, overtraining and where scaling laws break
md: Chinchilla-optimal answers one question: lowest loss per training FLOP. Real decisions also weigh inference volume, available data and downstream metrics, so production models are often smaller and trained on far more than 20 tokens per parameter.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Graded relevance and nDCG: rewarding the best result first
md: nDCG@k answers: what fraction of the best achievable discounted gain did the top k results capture? It is the default when labels are graded and users look mostly at the first page.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Why keyword match misses meaning and cross-encoders are too slow
md: Misconception: *semantic search understands meaning*. It finds vectors that are geometrically close, and closeness means whatever the training pairs rewarded. A model trained on question-answer pairs puts a question near its answer, not necessarily near a paraphrase of the question.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Why language models read subwords, not words or characters
md: A subword tokenizer gives you short sequences for common text **and** no unknown words, because anything rare can always fall back to smaller pieces. Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) is the most widely used way to choose those pieces.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Special tokens, chat templates and prompt boundaries
md: Hugging Face tokenizers match special-token strings in any text by default, the opposite of tiktoken. If user text is tokenized with them, escape it or load the tokenizer with `split_special_tokens=True`. Also, a rendered template already contains its special tokens: the Transformers docs say to tokenize it with `add_special_tokens=False` so they are not added twice.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Learning rate: the stability limit, warmup, decay and clipping
md: Clipping must go **after** `loss.backward()`, which computes the gradients, and **before** `optimizer.step()`, which applies the update. Andrej Karpathy (whose training recipe is lesson 8) keeps a list of silent bugs that includes clipping the *loss* instead of the gradients, which simply ignores outlier examples instead of taming their updates.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: HNSW, IVF, PQ and production indexes
lessonTitle: Greedy search on a proximity graph, and why ef matters
md: $ef$ is the size of the result list W. A larger $ef$ explores more of the graph, escapes more local minima and raises recall, at the cost of more distance computations. To return $k$ results you need $ef \ge k$; hnswlib (the reference C++ and Python implementation of HNSW) documents that ef cannot be set lower than k.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: The software supply chain: a map with every attack point
md: Every stage is a trust boundary, and attackers pick the stage with the widest fan-out: one poisoned library, build server or CI action reaches thousands of victims at once. Defence means asking, for each arrow, what proves the thing arriving is the thing you expected.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Provenance and SLSA levels: a signed record of how it was built
md: Provenance moves the question from 'do I trust this file?' to 'do I trust this repository, this workflow and this build platform?', which you can check by machine. npm's documentation is explicit that provenance does not guarantee a package has no malicious code; it makes origin verifiable.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Replace versus accumulate: what keeps the error bounded
md: Accumulation is not a free pass. The bound depends on the original real data never being thrown away, and on synthetic data being added on top rather than diluting a fixed budget: a variant that trains on n times more pure synthetic data still diverges, only more slowly (logarithmically). MAD also reports that a fixed real set only delayed degradation in its image experiments.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them
md: A system call is a mode switch plus cache pollution, paid per call. Make fewer, bigger calls (buffering, vectored I/O, batching) and let the vDSO serve the hottest read-only queries without entering the kernel.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Shared memory between processes: MAP_SHARED, shm_open and memfd
md: To share writable memory, both processes need `MAP_SHARED` mappings of the same pages: anonymous before `fork`, a `shm_open` name, or a memfd descriptor. Then order the accesses with release and acquire atomics or a lock; the mapping itself guarantees no ordering at all.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Measuring correctly: intended start times and HdrHistogram
md: Latency = completion time minus *intended* start time. The intended start comes from a load plan that does not depend on how fast the server answers.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: 5G identity privacy: SUPI, SUCI and ECIES concealment
md: SUCI encrypts the subscriber part of the identity under the home network's public key with a fresh ephemeral key each time, so listeners can neither read nor link it. It only works if the operator provisions the key and the phone cannot be downgraded.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: GNSS: how a receiver finds position and time, and what jamming does
md: A GNSS receiver solves for position and its own clock from at least four pseudoranges. Jamming removes the signals and is loud; spoofing replaces them and can be quiet, and a uniform delay shifts time without moving the position.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
